site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3647:          text: "Base-rate/reference class: recent official IRS annual inflation adjustments for this exact parameter show the base moving from the old $2,000 regime to $2,200 under Public Law 119-21, with TY2026 still $2,200 because the first year of chained-CPI growth over the 2024 base did not produce a full $100 rounded-down increase. site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3651:          text: "Simple discrete nowcast prior: using the May 2026 chained-CPI momentum and the remaining June-August window, I assign roughly 25 percent to a $2,200 IRS print, 60 percent to $2,300, 12 percent to $2,400, and 3 percent to policy or inflation outcomes outside that range. I do not use a richer time-series model because the rounded statutory threshold dominates the forecast and only three monthly CPI inputs remain before the formula is fixed.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3655:          text: "Mechanism decomposition: level is the statutory $2,200 base; momentum comes from elevated 2026 inflation, especially the May 2026 C-CPI-U 4.0 percent 12-month increase; the one-off component is energy-price pressure that may fade before August; policy risk is small because Public Law 119-21 already made the credit permanent, but Congress could still amend section 24 before the IRS print.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3659:          text: "Counter-consideration: the no-change $2,200 case remains plausible if June-August chained CPI is soft enough, if preliminary C-CPI-U revisions lower the 12-month average, or if IRS applies a technical convention that leaves the cumulative adjustment just below the $100 threshold. An upside outside the interval would require a legislative expansion or unusually high inflation producing a $2,500-or-higher official value; a downside outside the interval would require repeal or a statutory cut.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3663:          text: "Threshold math: under section 24(i)(2)-(3), the TY2027 increase is floor_to_$100(2200 * COLA_2027_with_2024_base). The first $100 increment requires COLA >= 100 / 2200 = 4.545 percent. TY2026 remained $2,200, implying the one-year 2025-over-2024 COLA generated less than $100 after rounding. By May 2026, BLS reported C-CPI-U +4.0 percent over 12 months and CPI-U +4.2 percent, so the two-year 2026-over-2024 window is likely above 4.545 percent by August 2026. The 80 percent interval of $2,200 to $2,400 corresponds to the central 97 percent of the discrete prior after excluding only the low-probability legislative-cut and $2,500-plus inflation-tail cases; the point is the modal rounded amount, $2,300.",

site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:7458:          text: "Counter-consideration: headline all-items CPI can move more than core measures because fresh food, energy, and subsidy timing can shift the monthly YoY rate; this keeps the interval wider than the recent four-month range.",

site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:19244:          text: "Point: 994 dollars FY2026 anchor x 1.027 May food-at-home momentum = 1020.8, rounded to 1021 dollars. Interval: translate uncertainty around June 2026 TFP movement, publication rounding down to whole dollars, and modest policy/mechanical risk into about +0.6% to +6.1% from the 994 anchor, giving 994 x 1.006 = 1000 and 994 x 1.061 = 1055. This is wider than the ERS 1.4% to 4.4% food-at-home prediction interval because the resolver is the TFP basket, not CPI itself, and because policy or basket-specific food movements can add tail risk.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:19248:          text: "Catalog-prior reconciliation: the local prior point of 1010 and CI of 975 to 1045 looked too low after incorporating the 994 FY2026 anchor plus May 2026 food-at-home CPI at 2.7 percent and ERS 2026 food-at-home midpoint at 2.8 percent, so I shift the point up to 1021 and move the interval to 1000 to 1055 while keeping a similar uncertainty width.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:19252:          text: "Counter-consideration: below 1000 would require roughly less than +0.6 percent growth from the FY2026 anchor, plausibly from a sharp June 2026 TFP softening or a policy freeze/rebase. Brier is the forecast-accuracy agent trained\nand evaluated inside that lab.\n\nThe point is not to build another human prediction market. The point is to\nmake millions of small, checkable forecasts over official series, publish the\nfull agent trace for each one, resolve them mechanically from official sources,\nand use proper scores to improve the agents.\n\n## Mission\n\nThesis exists to turn public decision-making into an empirical, auditable\nforecasting problem:\n\n1. Generate many forecast specs over official public data.\n2. Run AI agents only; no human forecasters, hidden priors, or private edits.\n3. Publish the prompt, command, stdout/stderr, fetched-source trace, normalized\n   forecast, validation report, resolution event, and score.\n4. Resolve from official first prints or explicitly defined policy states.\n5. Train and compare agents by forecast accuracy, not by preference ratings.\n\nThe long-run Brier goal is an open-source AI forecasting agent optimized\ndirectly for accuracy under proper scoring rules. In the ideal version, Brier\nlearns policies for source selection, base-rate construction, pack use,\ndistribution sizing, and final forecasts from scored Thesis runs. The reward is\nforecast accuracy. Humans still choose their goals and values; the agent's job\nis to give the best available predictions.\n\n## Scope\n\nThesis prioritizes targets that are:\n\n- published by government or similarly authoritative public institutions;\n- numeric, dated, and repeatedly released;\n- resolvable from a stable official source URL or release calendar;\n- suitable for first-print rules, fixed-vintage rules, or exact policy-state\n  checks;\n- high volume enough to create a training/evaluation environment.\n\nGood targets include labor-market releases, CPI and PCE releases, GDP and\nincome releases, Treasury and fiscal tables, administrative performance\nseries, central-bank policy settings, and clean international statistical\nagency releases.\n\nLower-priority targets include one-off news events, private-company outcomes,\nquestions requiring subjective judging, questions whose source can disappear,\nand questions where resolution needs a human committee.\n\n## Non-Goals\n\nThesis is not:\n\n- a place for humans to enter forecasts;\n- a Manifold/Metaculus clone;\n- a general chat assistant;\n- a collection of plausible mock traces;\n- a dashboard whose data can be hand-edited after the fact;\n- an RLHF preference benchmark.\n\nHuman review can improve code, schemas, and source coverage, but the forecasts\nthemselves should be produced by recorded agents and scored against official\noutcomes.\n\n## Forecast Cell Contract\n\nEvery forecast cell must answer four questions:\n\n- What exactly is being forecast?\n- When and where does it resolve?\n- What did the agent fetch and compute this run?\n- How should it be scored later?\n\nThat means every real forecast needs:\n\n- a stable `dataPointId`;\n- a `resolutionDate` verified from an official calendar or schedule;\n- a `resolutionSourceUrl` pointing to the official resolving source;\n- a first-print, fixed-vintage, or policy-state `resolutionRule`;\n- point estimate, 80% interval, and distribution;\n- trace steps with fetched numbers, base rate, math, counter-consideration,\n  and final forecast;\n- immutable activity artifacts.\n\nIf a target cannot be resolved mechanically, it should not enter the core\nThesis training environment.\n\n## Activity Trace Requirement\n\nThe trace is the scientific record. A highlighted reasoning summary is not\nenough.\n\nA production run should preserve:\n\n- prompt;\n- command and model invocation;\n- stdout and stderr;\n- raw Codex/agent event streams, last assistant message, and usage metadata\n  when the backend exposes them;\n- draft response, reviewer critique, revision prompt, and public disposition\n  when pre-submit review is enabled;\n- raw response;\n- parsed and normalized forecast JSON;\n- validation report;\n- manifest;\n- later resolution event and score.\n\nRuns that cannot satisfy the trace-depth rubric should remain as failed\nrecords, not be silently cleaned up into successful forecasts.\n\nThe app can display a simplified public reasoning trace, but the underlying\nrecord should preserve the complete machine trace needed to replay, audit, and\nscore the run.\n\n## Packs\n\nPacks are experimental forecasting interventions, not generic markdown skills.\n\nA pack should encode a reusable forecasting move such as release-vintage\ncalibration, base-rate construction, component decomposition, source\nselection, policy-mechanism decomposition, or known agency-specific resolution\nrules. Packs matter because they let Thesis compare agents and runs with and\nwithout the intervention on the same target family.\n\nPack pages should show what the pack changes in the forecast process and where\nit is used. They should not repeat a generic definition of what packs are on\nevery page.\n\n## Promoting Pack Insights\n\nWhen a pack consistently improves held-out forecast accuracy, its general\nforecasting lesson should stop being optional. Promote it into the default\nBrier/thesis.analyst system prompt, a universal skill, or the tool policy, then\nbump the agent version so future runs are attributable to the new default.\n\nPromotion is reserved for portable practices such as treating the base rate as\nthe prior forecast, frequent updates when new official information arrives,\nexplicit decomposition, benchmark competition against naive persistence, and\nrealized-volatility interval sizing. Domain-specific sources and priors should\nusually remain packs or skills so they can still be ablated.\n\nThe promotion gate is documented in\n[`docs/pack-promotion.md`](pack-promotion.md). Old runs remain valid; prompt\nhashes, tool-policy hashes, pack labels, and agent versions separate the\nexperimental regime from the promoted default.\n\n## Prioritization\n\nWhen choosing what to build or forecast next, prefer:\n\n1. More automatically resolvable official-series targets.\n2. Targets resolving soon enough to score the loop.\n3. Families with repeated releases and many comparable targets.\n4. Runs that compare agent versions, prompt modes, or pack sets.\n5. Infrastructure that reduces hand-editing and preserves full traces.\n6. UI that makes run comparison, resolution, and scoring legible.\n\nDo not prioritize novelty over autoresolution. A boring weekly government\nseries that resolves cleanly is more valuable than an interesting bespoke\nquestion that cannot become training data.\n\n## Scoring and Brier\n\nThe Brier Lab export is the bridge from Thesis records to agent training:\n\n- rows are forecast runs;\n- unresolved rows carry no reward until the official fact lands;\n- resolved rows receive proper scores, currently normalized CRPS;\n- split assignment is by `resolutionDate`, not run order;\n- training must avoid leakage from future official outcomes.\n\nThis makes Thesis a dataset and evaluation loop for Brier. Prompt experiments,\npack ablations, tool policies, and eventually RL policies should be judged by\nheld-out forecast accuracy.\n\n## Agent Operating Rule\n\nWhen a future agent is unsure what to do, the default answer should be:\n\n1. Add or improve automatically resolvable public-data forecasts.\n2. Preserve or improve full activity traces.\n3. Make comparison across agents, prompt modes, and pack sets easier.\n4. Make resolution and scoring more automatic.\n5. Keep the project open-source and reproducible.\n\nEverything else is secondary.\n", "exit_code": 0, "status": "completed"}}

I use 13.4 percent as the current-policy outside-view anchor before adding the conditional $3,000 fully refundable CTC.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2635:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Time-series prior: I do not extrapolate a simple linear trend because the child SPM series has large policy discontinuities from pandemic stimulus, expanded refundable credits, and their expiration; a persistence prior around the recent non-expanded-CTC level is more defensible.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2639:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Policy mechanism: a fully refundable $3,000 CTC would count in SPM tax-credit resources for eligible families and would matter most for children in low-earnings households who receive little or no current-law nonrefundable credit. Subtract 4.7 percentage points for the $3,000 fully refundable CTC, smaller than the 7.2 point 2021-to-2022 child SPM reversal because this condition excludes stimulus and the $3,600 young-child amount. Point = 13.4 - 4.7 = 8.7. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.\\\\\\\",\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: \\\\\\\"Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.\\\\\\\",\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: \\\\\\\"Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete.
